source_refs.note: Book p. 177: unit introduction, 10.1 distance formula (two forms), Example 1 (i)-(ii). No book errors on this page. Teaching notes, Key points and Common mistakes are ours.

blocks.text: In this unit we first establish the fundamental law of trigonometry and then use it to discuss the Trigonometric Identities. For this we need the formula for the distance between two points in a plane.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: An identity is an equation that is true for every value of the angle, for example \(\sin^{2}\theta + \cos^{2}\theta = 1\). Almost every identity in this unit is built from one result, the fundamental law \(\cos(\alpha - \beta) = \cos\alpha\cos\beta + \sin\alpha\sin\beta\) (topic 10.1.1). Its proof compares the lengths of two chords of a circle, which is why we first recall the distance formula.
Let \(P(x_{1}, y_{1})\) and \(Q(x_{2}, y_{2})\) be two points. If \(d\) denotes the distance between them, then

blocks.text_alt: d equals the length of PQ equals the square root of (x1 minus x2) squared plus (y1 minus y2) squared
or d equals the square root of (x2 minus x1) squared plus (y2 minus y1) squared

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Where does the formula come from? Join \(P\) and \(Q\) and complete a right-angled triangle with one horizontal and one vertical side. The horizontal side is \(|x_{2} - x_{1}|\), the vertical side is \(|y_{2} - y_{1}|\), and \(PQ\) is the hypotenuse, so by Pythagoras' theorem \(d^{2}\) is the sum of their squares.\nBoth forms give the same answer because \((x_{1} - x_{2})^{2} = (x_{2} - x_{1})^{2}\): squaring removes the sign, so the order of subtraction does not matter. A distance is never negative, so we always take the positive square root.

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.problem:
Find distance between the following points:
(i) \(A(3, 8)\), \(B(5, 6)\)
(ii) \(P(\cos x, \cos y)\), \(Q(\sin x, \sin y)\)
steps:
Given: (i) \(A(3, 8)\) and \(B(5, 6)\); (ii) \(P(\cos x, \cos y)\) and \(Q(\sin x, \sin y)\).
To find: the distance between the two points in each part.
Method: the distance formula \(d = \sqrt{(x_{1}-x_{2})^{2} + (y_{1}-y_{2})^{2}}\). It needs only the coordinates of the two points, which both parts give us.

Part (i), step 1: Name the coordinates
\[x_{1} = 3,\ y_{1} = 8\]
\[x_{2} = 5,\ y_{2} = 6\]
Why: writing the four numbers down first stops us from mixing an \(x\)-value with a \(y\)-value.

Part (i), step 2: Substitute and simplify
\[|AB| = \sqrt{(3-5)^{2} + (8-6)^{2}}\]
\[= \sqrt{(-2)^{2} + 2^{2}}\]
\[= \sqrt{4 + 4} = \sqrt{8}\]
\[= 2\sqrt{2}\]
Why: \((-2)^{2} = 4\) because a square is never negative, and \(\sqrt{8} = \sqrt{4 \times 2} = 2\sqrt{2}\).

Part (ii), step 1: Name the coordinates
\[x_{1} = \cos x,\ y_{1} = \cos y\]
\[x_{2} = \sin x,\ y_{2} = \sin y\]
Why: the formula works in exactly the same way when the coordinates are trigonometric expressions instead of numbers.

Part (ii), step 2: Substitute
\[|PQ| = \sqrt{(\cos x - \sin x)^{2} + (\cos y - \sin y)^{2}}\]
For the working we look at the quantity under the root, \(|PQ|^{2}\):
\[|PQ|^{2} = (\cos x - \sin x)^{2}\]
\[\quad + (\cos y - \sin y)^{2}\]
Why: it is easier to expand the squares first and take the root once at the end.

Part (ii), step 3: Expand each square
\[(\cos x - \sin x)^{2}\]
\[= \cos^{2}x + \sin^{2}x - 2\cos x\sin x\]
\[(\cos y - \sin y)^{2}\]
\[= \cos^{2}y + \sin^{2}y - 2\cos y\sin y\]
Why: \((a - b)^{2} = a^{2} + b^{2} - 2ab\).

Part (ii), step 4: Use \(\sin^{2}\theta + \cos^{2}\theta = 1\)
\[\cos^{2}x + \sin^{2}x = 1,\ \cos^{2}y + \sin^{2}y = 1\]
\[|PQ|^{2} = 2 - 2\cos x\sin x - 2\cos y\sin y\]
\[= 2 - 2(\cos x\sin x + \cos y\sin y)\]
Why: the squared terms pair up into two copies of the basic identity, each equal to 1; then we take 2 common from the last two terms, as the book does.

Part (ii), step 5: Take the square root
\[|PQ| = \sqrt{2 - 2(\cos x\sin x + \cos y\sin y)}\]
Why: the distance is the positive square root of \(|PQ|^{2}\). This is the form in which the book leaves the answer.

Check:
(i) From \(A(3, 8)\) to \(B(5, 6)\) we move 2 units across and 2 units down: the diagonal of a square of side 2, whose length is \(2\sqrt{2}\).
(ii) Put \(x = y = 0\): then \(P(1, 1)\) and \(Q(0, 0)\), whose distance is \(\sqrt{1 + 1} = \sqrt{2}\). Our answer gives \(\sqrt{2 - 2(0 + 0)} = \sqrt{2}\). Both agree.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. Distance between \(P(x_{1}, y_{1})\) and \(Q(x_{2}, y_{2})\): \(d = \sqrt{(x_{1}-x_{2})^{2} + (y_{1}-y_{2})^{2}}\).
2. The order of subtraction does not matter, because the differences are squared.
3. The coordinates may be numbers or trigonometric expressions; the method is the same.
4. With trigonometric coordinates, look for \(\sin^{2}\theta + \cos^{2}\theta = 1\) to simplify.
5. This formula is the tool used to prove the fundamental law in 10.1.1.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Taking the root of each term separately: \(\sqrt{a^{2} + b^{2}} \ne a + b\). For example \(\sqrt{4 + 4} = 2\sqrt{2}\), not \(2 + 2\).
2. Writing \((-2)^{2} = -4\). The square of a negative number is positive.
3. Subtracting an \(x\)-coordinate from a \(y\)-coordinate. Always pair \(x\) with \(x\) and \(y\) with \(y\).
